arxiv_submission.title: DistCat: A 2-Categorical Framework for Distance Derivation from First Principles
arxiv_submission.abstract: We present DistCat, a 2-categorical framework for deriving distance functions from first principles. The central principle states that any distance function δ on an observation space is derived from a more fundamental distance Γ on a source category via a natural transformation η: δ ⇒ Γ. We define DistCat as a 2-category whose 0-objects are base structures B=(C,F,O), 1-morphisms are structure-preserving functors with natural transformations, and 2-morphisms are distance-exporting pairs (Γ,δ). We prove the existence of a 2-functor D: DistCat → Met mapping base structures to metric spaces, and prove observation infeasibility: distinct base structures may yield isometric observation spaces. We prove the distance export functor D is well-defined on all five examples, including a complete 2-category axiom verification for the EMRI case. We verify the framework with five independently-motivated examples: (1) D1-grav-waves, reconstructing the Hellings-Downs correlation as a natural transformation in Extended Functorial AQFT; (2) D16+D24, deriving semantic geodesics from Fisher information geometry; (3) Bayesian inference, as Fisher-Rao distance under marginalization; (4) D26, formalizing resonance amplification in control theory; (5) EMRI chaos, connecting dark matter halo perturbations to Lyapunov exponents. We prove three predictions for the EMRI example: unstable-orbital frequency scaling, GW amplitude proportionality to resonance coefficients, and a KAM-breakup square-root scaling law for the Lyapunov exponent. We establish distance equivalence between D1 and D16+D24 (asymptotic), between D26 and EMRI (structural), and between D1 and EMRI (through GW observational bridge). Furthermore, we prove that the Fisher-Rao distance is the unique optimal pre-distance maximizing mutual information I(Γ;δ) for exponential family observations, providing a universal optimality criterion. The critical exponents α∈{1.84,2.00,2.00,∞,0.50} belong to different universality classes but share the same categorical structure. The distance export principle δ=Φ(Γ) appears to be a categorical invariant, not a domain-specific accident.
